summary.heading: How standing waves form
summary.html:
• A standing wave forms when two identical waves (same frequency, wavelength and amplitude) travel in opposite directions and superpose, usually a wave and its reflection.
Travelling waveStanding wave
Energytransferred along the waveno net transfer; stored in the medium
Amplitudethe same everywherezero at nodes, maximum at antinodes
Phasechanges steadily along the wavein phase within a loop; antiphase across a node
Profilemoves at speed $v$stays in place

summary.heading: Nodes, antinodes, amplitude and phase
summary.html:
• Node: a point that never moves. Antinode: a point with the largest amplitude.
  • Node to node (or antinode to antinode) = $\frac{\lambda}{2}$; node to the nearest antinode = $\frac{\lambda}{4}$.
  • All points between two neighbouring nodes are in phase (different amplitudes); points in neighbouring loops are in antiphase, a phase difference of $\pi$.
  • All points oscillate at the same frequency, except nodes. Energy depends on amplitude squared, so antinodes have the most and nodes none.

summary.heading: Harmonics on strings and in pipes
summary.html:
• Boundary conditions: a fixed string end or a closed pipe end is a (displacement) node; a free string end or an open pipe end is an antinode.
  • Sound in a pipe is longitudinal: describe it with displacement nodes and antinodes (no pressure nodes or end corrections needed).
  • The lowest-frequency pattern is the first harmonic. The IB doesn't use "fundamental" or "overtone".
EndsExamples$\lambda_n$Harmonics
node–nodestring fixed at both ends; pipe closed at both ends$\dfrac{2L}{n}$all
antinode–antinodestring free at both ends; pipe open at both ends$\dfrac{2L}{n}$all
node–antinodestring with one free end; pipe closed at one end$\dfrac{4L}{n}$odd only
$$f_n = \frac{v}{\lambda_n} = \frac{nv}{2L} \quad\text{or}\quad \frac{nv}{4L}$$
  • These aren't in the data booklet: sketch the pattern and count the half- or quarter-wavelengths in $L$.
  • New for 2028 Derive $L = \frac{n\lambda}{2}$ (matching ends) or $L = \frac{n\lambda}{4}$ with $n$ odd (node–antinode), and see that these set the harmonic names: a pipe closed at one end has only the 1st, 3rd, 5th… harmonics, so the pattern after the first is the third harmonic.
  • Wave speed on a string depends on tension and mass per unit length: tighter or lighter strings play higher notes; a shorter vibrating length (pressing a fret) plays a higher note.
  • Resonance tube: the difference between two successive resonance lengths is $\frac{\lambda}{2}$, which cancels the error from the antinode sitting slightly above the open end. The tuning fork fixes the frequency.

summary.heading: Natural frequency and resonance
summary.html:
• The natural frequency $f_0$ is the frequency at which a system oscillates freely after one disturbance. Strings and pipes have one for each harmonic.
  • A periodic driving force causes a forced oscillation at the driving frequency $f$.
Resonance: when the driving frequency equals (or is very close to) the natural frequency, energy is transferred most efficiently and the amplitude is greatest.
  • The amplitude stops growing when the energy lost per cycle equals the energy supplied per cycle (conservation of energy).

summary.heading: Damping
summary.html:
• Damping is energy loss from an oscillating system (friction, air resistance, drag), which reduces the amplitude.
  • Light damping: keeps oscillating with gradually decreasing amplitude; period almost unchanged (a guitar string dying away).
  • Critical damping: returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating (car shock absorbers, soft-closing doors).
  • Heavy damping: no oscillation, but returns more slowly than critical (a pendulum in thick oil).
  • Resonance curve (amplitude against driving frequency): more damping gives a lower maximum amplitude, a broader peak, and a resonant (peak) frequency shifted slightly below $f_0$.
  • Damping does not change the natural frequency $f_0$, which depends only on the system.
  • Very low driving frequencies: small amplitude, following the pushes. Very high: amplitude falls towards zero.

summary.heading: Useful and destructive resonance
summary.html:
• Useful: musical instruments (and their hollow bodies), tuning a radio circuit to one station, quartz clocks, MRI scanners, and greenhouse gases absorbing infrared at their molecules' natural frequencies (B.2).
  • Destructive: footbridges driven by walkers (London's Millennium Bridge, fixed with dampers), buildings in earthquakes (tuned mass dampers, as in Taipei 101), vibrating machine parts (rubber mounts), a glass shattered by a loud note.
  • Reduced by adding damping or designing the natural frequency away from likely driving frequencies.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Saying a standing wave transfers energy.
  • Taking node to node as one wavelength (it is half; node to antinode is a quarter).
  • Saying all points of a standing wave have the same amplitude.
  • Calling the second pattern of a pipe closed at one end the "second harmonic" (it is the third).
  • Mixing up pipe ends: closed end = displacement node, open end = displacement antinode.
  • Using "fundamental" or "overtone".
  • Thinking the frequency changes with the air-column length in a resonance tube (the fork sets it).
  • Saying damping changes the natural frequency, or confusing critical and heavy damping.

Patterns and trends: Play two notes an octave apart (2 : 1) and then two that clash. Can students hear the pattern before they know the numbers?
Why is describing a pattern with numbers such an important step, even before anyone can explain it?
Models: The same "whole number of half-wavelengths" idea fits strings, pipes, microwave ovens and electrons in atoms. What does each system have in common that makes the model work?
Where does the model fail? (For example, real open pipes need an end correction.)
Observations: Chladni's sand made nodes visible. What other tricks do physicists use to make invisible things observable?
Does an observation made with a trick like this count as direct observation?
Global impact: Who should pay for damping a bridge after it is built: the designer, the owner or the public?
How might engineers in an earthquake zone decide what natural frequency to give a new building?

oracy.html:
Hot seat (whole class, 8 minutes): one student, the expert, answers the class's questions; swap experts every few questions. Situation: a violinist bows one open string gently, then harder and faster; the tension is unchanged. What happens to the pitch and the loudness?

  • My question for the expert is …
  • Could you explain why …?
  • What would happen if …?

Listen for: the frequency is set by the length, tension and mass per unit length, so the pitch stays the same; the amplitude grows, so it is louder.

Is music universal?: Ask students whether music from their own culture uses the same intervals as Western music. Does physics or culture decide what sounds pleasant?
Can a physical explanation of harmony ever explain why a piece of music is moving?
Can we know what we can't picture?: Students can picture a vibrating string but not an electron's standing wave. Is the second kind of knowledge weaker?
What role does mathematics play when imagination runs out?
Do words shape understanding?: Does "first harmonic" make the pattern $f_1, 3f_1, 5f_1$ easier to understand than "fundamental and first overtone"?
Find other words that mean different things in physics and everyday life (resonance, damping, work). Can they cause misconceptions?
Should we learn from failure?: Engineers learned a great deal from the Millennium Bridge and the Tacoma Narrows collapse. Should such risks ever be accepted as part of learning?
Is knowledge from an accident less reliable than knowledge from a planned experiment, or just harder to repeat?

videos.title: Singing plates - Standing Waves on Chladni plates
videos.use: Sand collects along the nodes of a vibrating plate. Use it with the Observations NoS idea, and ask students where the nodes and antinodes are.

videos.title: Shattering a Wine Glass with Sound at 187,500FPS - The Slow Mo Guys
videos.use: Slow-motion footage of a glass driven at its natural frequency. A memorable example of destructive resonance: ask what happens to the amplitude each cycle.

videos.title: The Tacoma Narrows Fallacy
videos.use: Extension: explains why the famous bridge collapse is not a simple case of resonance. Good for the ToK question on learning from failure and for checking textbook claims.

alsoLabs.note: One question asks whether the slowly decreasing amplitude changes the period: an example of light damping. The lab's main topic is C.1.
